Free version transcription block of unreadable text. I wanted to try an AI to transcribe meetings for my nonprofit, since it is legally required, and would simplify note taking. The transcription seemed to work well too, but the free version is setup so that if you export, or copy/paste, you lose 100% of the formatting and end up with  a massive unreadable block of text.  You can use other AI tools to at least separate different speakers, but different dialogue from an individual speakers is still all mashed together in a massive paragraph (imagine if some one presents for awhile).  As well, there is no functional, like a scroll bar, to allow users review the transcript in the app, so you can only see the last few lines of dialogue from the meeting.  My guess this is all to incentivize people to buy upgrades, but if an app cannot perform the basics, why would I expect upgrades to be better.  After looking around at tools, I am disappointed such a highly rated app performed so poorly, and I would recommend Granola rethink offering a free version with such limitations.

Granola has quietly become the most indispensable app on my Mac.. I've tried many meeting recorder and note-taking tool out there, and nothing comes close. What separates Granola from everything else is the philosophy behind it. It doesn't join your meeting as a bot, doesn't awkward-sit in the corner of your video call, doesn't require anyone's permission or awareness. It just listens and works. That alone is worth five stars.

The post-meeting summaries are wonderful - structured, readable, and actually reflective of what was discussed rather than a word-salad transcript with bullet points slapped on top. And the built-in AI lets you interrogate your own meetings afterward: pull a specific decision, reconstruct an action item list, answer "wait, what did we actually agree to?" The answers are good.

For power users: the MCP integration is a game-changer. Hooking Granola into your own LLM workflows means your meeting history becomes a living knowledge base, not a graveyard of forgotten notes.

If it's not obvious from the title, I'm a VC and I spend a ton of time in meetings with founders. What's less obvious is all the other things. After treading water for at least a decade, I am deeply suspect of any VC's organizational capabilities. Mostly my own. Believe it or not, for the longest time, my notes lived in saved (and unsaved) text files in Sublime Text. At some point I've tried using TiddlyWiki, bandwagoned onto Notion and Obsidian, and once even opened Microsoft OneNote. My brain doesn't work like that, the 5,715 unread emails in my inbox is proof of a losing battle. Asana helped, I tried sprint planning like my time working for a startup, but I quickly learned you can’t budget 10 points for firefighting. A more recent addition has been Granola, great UI, but I realize I actually don't find AI notetakers helpful. If you can imagine, I look at 2,000 companies a year, and meet just under a quarter of them, at some point they all start to blend together. Logseq came the closest, the daily journal clicked for me, but I wanted mobile, reliable sync, and a search that didn’t need the gentle touch of a crowbar. I love you Logseq team. <3 So I built a tool of my own, DayCarp (daycarp.com) it’s a minimalist notetaker with Sublime’s minimap, Granola’s AI notetaking, Logseq’s journal, and some of Asana’s tasking. It also has nice quality of life features like inline images, templates, Excel-style calculations when you highlight numbers, and of course AI, bring your own API key, self-host, or use mine. Go to DayCarp.com and try it free, would appreciate the roast. It’s something I genuinely use every day, and I think others might find useful. Here’s how I take notes in a meeting with a founder: 1. I setup my framework with these headings: Team, Product, Business Model, IP/Regulatory, Market, Competition, Traction, Financing, Decision & Next Steps. This is my mental framework, and also roughly the order by which I ask questions. I start with getting to know the people, and end with the financing discussion. It’s not unlike a sales call from the VC side as well, we need to sell great founders as much as founders need great VCs. 2. Under each heading I put a bullet or two about things I learned about the company after spending all of 45 seconds looking at their deck or website. I usually also put one or two things in common with the founder that I can bring up in conversation. 3. I put “Q: [question]”; under each bullet where I want to push the founder, for tech-heavy pre-revenue startups I might push on IP, or problem; for a classic SaaS, I’ll try to push on quality of traction. I’ll also try to size the market to get an idea, founders often share a massive number in an unrelated market. 4. If I don’t have much time, I’ll pitch the startup back to the founder “I understand you do XYZ for so and so, did I understand that correctly?”, that saves about 10 minutes off the pitch. I’ll also preface that I’m conversational and that we might jump around, to avoid the pitch entirely. All founders have a narrative and a story they want to tell, and they’ll tactfully try to avoid their weaknesses, the purpose of the structure is to make sure I hit the parts the matter. 5. The hardest to evaluate, and the most important are teams, their motivations, ambitions, vision, how they work with others, there’s a lot you miss in a first meeting. 6. I’ll write down my impression and decision right at the end. I will communicate this to my team when we review pipeline. I like using AI notes features here, to help close some of the gaps, typically I miss some of the customer names, or an offhand comment about a partnership. 7. I delete the note and blacklist the founder if they don't mention AI, Andreessen or Sequoia. --Alex

That is, saying we have a "context graph" is just marketing speak, it doesn't really add any new possibility or feature that isn't possible from using other search and database tools. Also, this kind of tool, using AI to extract a decision from Granola for example, is possible to one-shot prompt. I.e. you don't need any special tool to do it, you just need a single prompt. Granola itself has this kind of functionality. I think you're trying to solve a problem that doesn't really exist, what surface patterns are you going to uncover that someone don't know to look for? Either there is a todo from a meeting or note or email or there isn't. Writing notes or prep for a meeting isn't rocket science, and you don't need a graph database to "surface patterns" to prepare your pre-meeting notes. If you use something like Granola, 99% of the time (or maybe 100% really), the Granola summary is all you need. If you want something more you copy the whole transcript and send it to Claude for some specific reason. Graphiti is primarily focused on extracting and organizing structured facts into a knowledge graph. Rowboat is more focused on day-to-day work. We organize the graph around people, projects, organizations, and topics. One design choice we made was to make each node human-readable and editable. For example, a project note contains a clear summary of its current state derived from conversations and tasks across tools like Gmail or Granola. It’s stored as plain Markdown with Obsidian-style backlinks so the user can read, understand, and edit it directly.

Another thing I'd suggest: look into and use non-coding AI tools that improve productivity. For example: Zoom meeting transcriptions and summaries or Granola. A lot of context is lost when you take manual notes in meetings. If you use a tool that turns a meeting into notes automatically, you can use those notes to bootstrap a prompt/plan for agents.

I think it's important to start with identifying your bottlenecks, and work from there to determine the solutions you need. In the case of our business, I feel that my time is best spent talking to customers and prospects. These discussions directly impact revenue, retention, product strategy, etc. So then I start thinking ... what sort of things am I doing that take me away from talking to customers? I spend a lot of time on implementation. I spend a lot of time on administrative sales tasks (chasing people for meetings, writing proposals, negotiating contracts). I spend a lot of time on meeting prep and follow-up. And many more. So I'm always on the hunt for tools with a problem already in mind. In terms of specific tools... Claude is a great backbone for a lot. Both the chatbot but also the API. I use the chatbot to help me write proposals and review contracts. I used it to write scripting to automate our implementation process which was once quite manual and is now a button click. Cursor has been a game changer. In particular, it means that we spend very little time on bugfixes and small features. This keeps my CTO almost 100% focused on big picture needle-moving projects. We are now doing some research into things like Codex/Claude Code to see how we could improve this further. Another app that I really love is called Granola. It automatically joins all of my meetings, writes notes, reminds me what promises I made, helps me write follow-up emails, and helps me prep for meetings. Finally, we use an email client called Sedna (disclaimer: I used to work at Sedna) which is fully programmable. We've been building our own internal tooling (leveraging the Claude API) on top of Sedna to help automate different workflows. For example, my inbox is now perfectly prioritised. In many cases, when I receive emails from customers, an AI has already written a draft that I can review and send. I know there are a lot of out-of-the-box tools out there like Fyxer to help with things like this, but I've really appreciated the ability to get exactly what we want by building certain things ourselves.

So I made my own dictation app. Supports arbitrary API providers (e.g. Deepgram, Speechmatics, Elevenlabs), Offline models and a subscription if you want it. Otherwise it's free forever for BYOK and offline models. Deepgram is a YC startup from 2016, and have models that are genuinely good - so it's up to you if you want to use them. Also, Granola doesn't let you read your own meetings after 30 days. So I added a feature in DuckType to import your data from Granola, unlocking all your meetings from their paywall. Hey HN; I’m the solo founder of Loreo. I built this because I wanted a meeting tool that actually acted like a ‘COO’ for my projects; not just a passive listener. Why I built this: I was frustrated with the current ‘bot-in-the-middle’ era of meeting apps. Most tools (Fireflies/Otter) require a ‘bot guest’ that announces itself and kills the vibe. I also found that tools like Granola were great... but they delete your raw audio after transcribing. If the AI hallucinations happen; you have no way to verify. What makes Loreo different? 1. Contextual AI: You can chat with a single recording or an entire series of past meetings. You can ask ‘What were the pending action items from the last three syncs?’ across your whole history. 2. Audio Ownership: Loreo keeps your audio playback and allows file uploads of existing recordings. 3. Privacy/Efficiency: Built with Tauri v2 (Rust). It’s a local ~8MB app that captures system audio directly. No ‘bot guest’ required; and your audio stays under your control. 4. Modern Engine: We use ElevenLabs Scribe v2; which is significantly more accurate for non-English languages (we are currently focused on the Japanese and Korean markets).
